neighbours.label: a physical property or detectable signal named in natural-science exposition (brightness, densities, gravity, radar, migration of a protein), not the same word in everyday use
fire: Spectrographs recorded a shift in wavelength as the galaxy receded from the telescope.
The rover's instrument measures how the soil conducts heat during the cold Martian night.
Ice in the crater floors reflects radar pulses more strongly than the bare regolith around it.
Jupiter's moons have densities that suggest rocky cores beneath their icy shells.
Labelled antibodies revealed the migration of the receptor from the membrane to the nucleus.
Variable stars change their brightness over periods of days or weeks.
Neutron star matter has a gravity so strong that light bends sharply around it.
Heavy water absorbs neutrons differently from ordinary water, which matters in a reactor.
quiet: The hall was bright with lanterns during the harvest festival.
Rural migration to the cities has reshaped the labour market since the 1950s.
The two cafés price their coffee differently, so students favour the cheaper one.
Police used a radar gun to catch speeding drivers on the bypass.
The report described population densities in the suburbs of Lyon.
The seriousness of the charges gave the hearing a particular gravity.
You will hear the choir rehearsing if you pass the chapel at noon.
The dancers were lighter on their feet after a week of rest.

predictions: fire 7-8 of 8 at 0.5-0.8; the same words in everyday or social contexts under 0.05; 'population densities' may leak a little
short: physical property/signal word in science prose
notes: Probe: brightness 0.647, differently (neutrons) 0.616, radar 0.602, densities 0.804, migration (protein) 0.807; same words outside science: bright coat 0.009, bird migration festival 0.023, ledgers formatted differently 0.034; budget floor 0.011. The pole fires on the measurable-property word only when the sentence is physical-science exposition.
